lead: In a flotilla the lead boat shows the way, but the collision rules bind every skipper. You need a handful of them: keep a lookout, know when there is risk, know who keeps clear, and make your move early.

sections.title: Your own eyes, a steady bearing, an early turn

qa.q: How do I know if another boat is on a collision course with me?
qa.a: Take her compass bearing, then take it again a few minutes later. A **steady bearing** while she gets closer means **risk of collision**; in doubt, assume it, and keep clear early with one large alteration.

blocks.p: Following the lead boat does not hand over your watch. Every vessel keeps her own **lookout** by sight and hearing, all the time, astern and under the genoa too.

fig.note: Same bearing five minutes later, and closer

blocks.p: To see whether a vessel will hit you, take her compass bearing, then take it again a few minutes later. A steady bearing while she gets closer is **risk of collision**. In doubt, assume it.
When you keep clear, do it **early and boldly**: one large change of course or speed that she sees at once and that leaves a safe distance. Small alterations tell her nothing.

sections.title: Port tack keeps clear, then the windward boat

qa.q: Which yacht gives way when two boats under sail are converging?
qa.a: The one on **port tack** keeps clear of the one on starboard tack; on the same tack the **windward** boat keeps clear. A boat overtaking from astern keeps clear of everyone, whatever the tacks.

blocks.p: Your **tack** is the side the wind comes over. When two boats under sail converge, the one on **port tack** keeps clear. On the same tack the **windward** boat keeps clear.

tiles.name: Opposite tacks
tiles.note: you are on port tack: keep clear

tiles.name: Same tack
tiles.note: she is to windward: she keeps clear

blocks.p: **Overtaking** comes first. If you catch another vessel up from astern, you keep clear until you are past, whatever the tacks and whether she is sail or power.

fig.note: Faster and coming up from astern: you keep clear

blocks.rule: Port tack gives way to starboard tack, windward to leeward, and the overtaking boat to everyone.

sections.title: Head-on, crossing, and when you stand on

qa.q: Who gives way when two motor boats are crossing?
qa.a: The vessel that has the other on her **starboard side** gives way: she turns to starboard to pass astern, or slows, and does not cross ahead. Meeting head-on, both turn to starboard and pass port to port.

blocks.p: Under engine you are a power-driven vessel. Meeting **head-on**, both turn to starboard and pass port to port. **Crossing**, the one that has the other on her starboard side gives way: she turns to starboard to pass astern, or slows, and does not cross ahead.

tiles.name: Crossing
tiles.note: she is on your starboard side: you give way

blocks.p: With the other vessel on your port side you are the **stand-on vessel**: hold your course and speed. If she does not act, sound five short blasts. If she still comes on, act yourself: slow down, stop or turn to starboard, never to port towards her.

qa.q: Does a yacht motor-sailing have to give way to boats under sail?
qa.a: Yes: with the engine in gear your yacht is a **power-driven vessel**, whatever sails are set, and keeps clear of boats under sail alone. By day she shows a black cone, point down, forward.

blocks.p: A **power-driven vessel** keeps clear of a vessel under sail, even one on her port side: the starboard-side rule is for two power vessels only. A sailing vessel in turn keeps clear of a vessel **engaged in fishing** with nets or a trawl.

tiles.name: Fishing
tiles.note: two cones, points together: keep clear

tiles.name: Motor-sailing
tiles.note: cone point down: she counts as power

blocks.p: The engine decides what you are. With it in gear your yacht is power-driven, whatever sails are set, and keeps clear of boats under sail alone. By day a motor-sailing yacht shows a black cone, point down, forward.

sections.title: Keep right and leave the ferry her water

qa.q: Do I have to keep clear of a ferry in a narrow channel when I'm sailing?
qa.a: Yes: a sailing vessel, and any vessel under 20 m, **must not impede** a vessel that can navigate only inside a **narrow channel** (Rule 9). Keep near the starboard edge and move to the side early.

blocks.p: In a **narrow channel**, a canal or a strait, keep as near to its starboard edge as is safe.

fig.note: She can only use the channel: move to the edge

blocks.p: A ferry or ship that can navigate only inside the channel has nowhere else to go. A sailing vessel, and any vessel under 20 m, **must not impede** her: "power gives way to sail" does not help you here. Move to the side early.

sections.title: Read the other boat from her lights

qa.q: What do I do if I see a vessel's red light on my starboard bow at night?
qa.a: Give way: that red is her port **sidelight**, so on a steady bearing she is crossing from your starboard side. Turn to starboard and pass astern of her.

blocks.p: A flotilla sails by day, but late arrivals happen. A boat under way shows a red **sidelight** to port, a green one to starboard and a white **sternlight**. A power-driven vessel adds a white **masthead light**, the steaming light, above them.

tiles.name: Power, crossing
tiles.note: red on your starboard bow: give way

tiles.name: Tricolour
tiles.note: one colour high up: sail, keep clear

blocks.p: Red is her port side. On your starboard bow, on a steady bearing, she is crossing from your starboard: turn to starboard and pass astern of her.
Under sail a yacht under 20 m may show the three colours in one **tricolour** at the masthead. Under engine switch on the steaming light, sidelights and sternlight, and the tricolour off.

sections.title: Short blasts in harbour, long ones in fog

qa.q: What do three short blasts from a ship or ferry mean?
qa.a: **My engines are going astern**: a ferry at the quay sounding three short blasts is backing out, so keep away from her stern. One short blast means altering course to starboard, two short to port.

blocks.p: A short blast lasts about one second, a prolonged blast four to six. Power-driven vessels in sight of one another signal their manoeuvres; in fog a vessel under way sounds her signal at least every two minutes.

head: Signal
Meaning
rows: I am altering course to starboard
I am altering course to port
I doubt you are doing enough to keep clear
Sailing, fishing or towing; not under command, restricted in her ability to manoeuvre or constrained by her draught

blocks.p: Three short blasts from a ferry at the quay: she is backing out, so keep away from her stern. A prolonged blast coming closer in fog is a vessel under power: slow down and listen.
